sentences.text: The genus Sarcosuchus includes the type species Sarcosuchus imperator and is classified within the family Pholidosauridae.
Sarcosuchus is most closely related to the North American genus Terminonaris, though a 2019 study placed it phylogenetically closer to Dyrosauridae within the group Tethysuchia.
However, a 2019 study placed Sarcosuchus phylogenetically closer to Dyrosauridae within the group Tethysuchia.

Fully grown S. imperator individuals are estimated to have reached lengths of 9 to 9.5 meters and weights of 3.45 to 4.3 metric tons, though O'Brien et al. (2019) estimated the largest specimen was nearly 9 meters long and weighed 3.45 metric tons.
The largest known skull of S. imperator measures 1.6 meters in length, leading to an estimated total body length of 11.65 meters.

Sarcosuchus possessed a very long skull with a snout that made up approximately 75% of the total cranial length, with the longest confirmed skull measuring 1.6 meters long and a snout measuring 115 cm in length and 270 mm in width.
This species had telescoped eyes and a snout that accounted for 75% of the skull's length.
Sarcosuchus vertebrae are amphicoelus, a feature not found in modern crocodilians or Atoposauridae.
Sarcosuchus osteoderms on the neck and back had low keels and hook-shaped extensions, while tail osteoderms lacked these features.
Sarcosuchus is considered a generalist predator, unlike most other pholidosaurids which were specialized fish eaters.
Fossils of Sarcosuchus were first discovered in the 1850s in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, by Samuel Allport.
The genus Sarcosuchus was first described in 1966 by Frances de Broin and Philippe Taquet based on an incomplete skull found in Gadoufaoua, northern Niger.
The species Sarcosuchus hartti was originally described by Marsh in 1869, and in 1977 the species formerly known as Crocodylus hartti was reassigned to the genus Sarcosuchus.
Researchers Sereno et al. used skull length measurements to estimate the size of Sarcosuchus because a complete skeleton was unavailable.

Isotopic analyses suggest that S. imperator had a diet consisting of both fish and large dinosaurs, and researchers hypothesized that Sarcosuchus imperator had a generalized diet including large terrestrial prey like dinosaurs.
Biomechanical analyses indicate that Sarcosuchus was not capable of performing a crocodile-like 'death roll'.
It is debated whether Sarcosuchus had a lifestyle similar to the Nile crocodile, hunting large terrestrial prey.
Sarcosuchus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically the Hauterivian to Albian ages, in North Africa and Brazil.
The Gadoufaoua locality, where Sarcosuchus fossils were found, dates to between 125 and 112 million years ago.
During the Early Cretaceous, North Africa and Brazil were covered in mangrove forests and wetlands, creating a biodiversity hotspot.
Some researchers argue that estimates of S. imperator size based on modern crocodilian correlations are significantly larger than reality.
